ai.definition: A Brain-Computer Interface for Augmented Reality (BCI-AR) is a technology that allows direct communication between the user's brain and an AR system, enabling seamless integration of augmented reality elements into the user’s visual and auditory experience.
ai.howItWorks: Sensors and neural interfaces capture brain signals which are then processed to understand the user's intentions or perceptions. This data is transmitted in real-time to an AR device that overlays digital information onto the user's environment, creating a more immersive and interactive experience.
ai.problemSolved: Enhancing human perception and interaction by integrating AR seamlessly into daily activities without requiring manual input from the user.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing highly sensitive sensors and neural interfaces, followed by integration with AR hardware. This requires precise engineering and material science to ensure both high sensitivity and reliability.
ai.buildProcess: Involves designing and testing sensor arrays, interfacing them with brain tissue, and calibrating the system for real-time data processing. The build process also includes integrating these components into wearable or implantable devices.
ai.costDrivers: High research and development costs due to the complexity of neural interfaces and AR technology. Manufacturing costs are driven by the precision required in sensor fabrication and integration with advanced computing hardware.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected to transition from lab research to early commercialization within the next few years as key technological hurdles are overcome.
ai.regulation: Currently under regulatory scrutiny, particularly concerning safety and privacy. Regulations will likely evolve as the technology matures.
ai.risks: Technological risks include achieving reliable and non-invasive brain signal capture. Safety concerns revolve around potential side effects from prolonged use or implantation. Ethical considerations around data privacy and consent are also significant.
ai.profitability: Potential for high profitability once commercialized, given the unique capabilities it offers in enhancing human interaction with digital information.
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected to see advancements in miniaturization of sensors, improvement in signal processing algorithms, and increased integration with AI for more sophisticated applications.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Power consumption will likely decrease as technology advances.

glossary.def: Devices that interact directly with the brain to capture or deliver signals.

subsystems.name: Neural sensor
subsystems.role: records the electrical activity the system decodes — from outside the skull, on the brain surface, or inside the cortex.
parts: ECoG electrode grids on the cortex

subsystems.name: Signal acquisition
subsystems.role: amplifies microvolt signals and strips out noise before decoding.

subsystems.name: Decoder
subsystems.role: turns raw signals into intent — a direction, a selection, a command.
parts: feature extraction (steady-state visual evoked potentials, P300 responses, motor-imagery rhythms, spike sorting)

subsystems.name: Neural write path
subsystems.role: delivers information back to the nervous system where the AR display cannot reach.

subsystems.name: AR display and audio
subsystems.role: presents the augmented visual and auditory layer that the BCI controls.

subsystems.name: Fusion and control loop
subsystems.role: merges gaze, head pose and decoded intent into one interaction model within a strict latency budget.

subsystems.name: Implant support (invasive versions)
subsystems.role: keeps the electrodes alive and safe inside the body for years.

buildSteps.title: Choose the interface class
buildSteps.detail: Non-invasive (headset), minimally invasive (electrodes delivered through blood vessels), or intracortical arrays requiring surgery. This decision fixes the achievable bandwidth.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the electrodes
buildSteps.detail: Micromachined silicon or polymer shanks, thin-film metal contacts on flexible substrates, or conductive hydrogel electrodes for a dry headset.

buildSteps.title: Package and connect
buildSteps.detail: Invasive devices are sealed in a hermetic case, leads are routed, and an inductive coil is fitted for power and data. Headsets get shielded wiring and active electrodes.

buildSteps.title: Build the acquisition electronics
buildSteps.detail: Amplifiers, digitisation and wireless transmission are integrated into a headstage small and light enough to wear or implant.

buildSteps.title: Build the AR optics
buildSteps.detail: Waveguides or combiners are assembled with the light engine and eye tracker, then characterised for field of view, brightness and latency.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the decoder to the user
buildSteps.detail: The person performs guided tasks while the system learns their individual signals; artefact rejection is tuned to their eye and muscle activity.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Decoded intent is mapped to AR actions — cursor movement, object selection, layer toggling — and latency and error rates are measured.

buildSteps.title: Add the write path (if used)
buildSteps.detail: Stimulation electrodes are mapped to perceived locations so that patterns of current produce useful phosphenes or other sensations.

buildSteps.title: Validate safety and usability
buildSteps.detail: Long-term recording stability, tissue response, thermal limits and everyday wearability are tested over months, not hours.

prerequisites.why: intracortical signals typically degrade over months to years as tissue reacts to the implant.
skull and tissue blur EEG signals, so non-invasive read-out is far too coarse for natural-feeling control.
a device must run for years on a small battery or wireless power without heating tissue.
intent must be inferred within tens of milliseconds to feel coupled to the display.

prerequisites.tech: Neural stimulation that produces useful perception
prerequisites.why: electrical stimulation of the visual cortex produces phosphenes, but at very low resolution.

prerequisites.tech: AR displays with wide field of view and low latency
prerequisites.why: headsets must be comfortable and fast enough to overlay on natural vision without lag.

pathway.milestone: non-invasive BCIs select and steer objects in AR/VR headsets using steady-state visual evoked potentials and motor imagery; intracortical arrays let paralysed participants type and move a cursor
pathway.unlocks: assistive control and a research interaction vocabulary.

pathway.milestone: medical BCI-AR systems: implanted arrays plus smart glasses that overlay cues, and cortical visual prostheses generating simple phosphene patterns
pathway.unlocks: restored communication and rudimentary sight for people with severe impairment.

pathway.milestone: minimally invasive, higher-channel-count electrodes delivered without open-skull surgery
pathway.unlocks: wider patient access and longer recording stability.

pathway.milestone: bidirectional closed-loop interfaces with thousands of safe, stable channels reading and writing in real time
pathway.unlocks: richer control and direct sensory feedback rather than a visual overlay alone.
the seamless everyday AR integration the concept promises; no method for this exists today.
